To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
gut microbial CutC is sufficient to transmit platelet reactivity in a host via trimethylamine/trimethylamine N-oxde production.

the gut microbial choline Tma-lyase pathway is a molecular target for the prevention of atherothombotic cardiovascular disease and that microbial cutC is sufficient to transmit the enhanced platelet reactivities and thrombotic potential associated with TMA/TMA production in a host.

microbial colonization studies using germ-free mice colonize with a defined CutC-expresscing human commensal (ie, Clostidium sporogeness &Dgr;CutC) demonstrate that CutC-dependent TMA generation is sufficient to transmit platelet reactivity, thrombosis potential and atherosclerotic plaque formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how gut microbes influence cardiovascular disease (CVD) and thrombosis risk.
the role of gut microbiota in cardiovascular disease.
the identification of microbial genes and pathways that contribute to the development of atherothombosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
microbial choline TMO-lyase-dependent TMA/TMO production is sufficient to enhance platelet reactivity in vivo, and thus may be a rational molecular target of treatment for atherothrombosis.
the gut microbial choline Tma-lyase pathway is a rational molecular target to reduce atherothrombosis risk.
the gut microbial choline Tma-lyase CutC is sufficient to transmit platelet hyperreactivity and thrombosis via Tma/TMAO.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
microbial TMA-lyse activity, in particular CutC, is sufficient to transmit platelet hyperreactivity and thrombosis risk in a host via the TMA/TMAo pathway.

gut microbial choline Tma-lyases are sufficient to transmit enhanced thrombosis potential to a host via Tma/Tmao generation and that microbial choline Tmalyases represent a rational molecular target to prevent and treat cardiovascular disease.
microbial choline Tma-lyase-dependent TMA/Tmao production is sufficient to promote a prothrombotic phenotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gut microbes containing cutC are sufficient to enhance platelet reactivity in vivo and transmit heightened thrombotic potential in a host.
the gut microbiota influences the host’s platelet function via the production of trimethlyamine (TMA).
the microbial choline utilization pathway is sufficient to transmit the enhanced platelet reactive phenotype and thrombosis phenotype observed with human gut microbial transplantation.
